# Normalized thin convex measures and compatible ball lifts

This note separates three facts. A single normalized thin-body limit
has an exact concave-density representation. Independently making
every fiber lift have volume one can destroy sampled convexity, even
when the original bodies were compatible. A common projection and a
common volume normalization preserve compatibility by a simultaneous
ball-fiber construction. None of these statements asserts continuity
of mixed halfspace depth under dimension collapse.

## 1. Exact single-measure classification

Let m>=1, let K_l be compact m-dimensional convex bodies in a fixed
Euclidean space R^D, D>=m, and let

    mu_l=H_m restricted to K_l / H_m(K_l).

The affine hulls of K_l may vary. Suppose mu_l converges weakly to a
probability measure mu. Let E=aff(supp mu), and put q=dim E. Then q<=m.

* If q=0, mu is a Dirac measure.
* If 1<=q<m, with r=m-q, mu has a density f relative to H_q on E,
  and h=f^(1/r) has a nonnegative concave representative on its convex
  support. That support is compact, and h has a bounded upper
  semicontinuous concave extension to its closure.
* If q=m, mu is normalized uniform volume on a q-dimensional convex
  body. This is the limiting infinite density-concavity exponent,
  not the formula 1/(m-q) with a finite denominator.

The exponent in the middle assertion is the DENSITY exponent
1/(m-q). The probability measure itself is 1/m-concave. These are
different parameters.

### Proof of closure and the exponent

Brunn--Minkowski gives, for compact sets A,B and 0<t<1,

    mu_l((1-t)A+tB)^(1/m)
       >=(1-t)mu_l(A)^(1/m)+t mu_l(B)^(1/m),       (1)

when both masses are positive. Indeed, the Minkowski average of
K_l intersect A and K_l intersect B is contained in
K_l intersect ((1-t)A+tB), all measured in aff(K_l).

Here is the weak-closure step, including the direction of Portmanteau.
For fixed compact A,B put S=(1-t)A+tB. For epsilon>0 let A^epsilon
and B^epsilon be their open epsilon neighborhoods. Their Minkowski
average lies in the CLOSED 2epsilon neighborhood S_[2epsilon].
Use (1) for these neighborhoods (or compact subsets approaching
their masses), the lower Portmanteau bound on the two open sets,
and the upper Portmanteau bound on S_[2epsilon]. This gives

    mu(S_[2epsilon])^(1/m)
       >=(1-t)mu(A)^(1/m)+t mu(B)^(1/m).

Let epsilon decrease to zero. Thus mu is 1/m-concave, and its support
is convex: positive neighborhoods of two support points have positive
mass in every intermediate neighborhood by this same inequality.

We now use the classical density characterization of concave measures:
on its q-dimensional affine support, an s-concave measure with
s<=1/q has a density whose concavity exponent is s/(1-sq); at
s=1/q that density is constant on its convex support. If s>1/q,
a non-Dirac measure with q-dimensional support is impossible. Applied
with s=1/m, this gives q<=m and precisely 1/(m-q) when q<m.
This is Borell's characterization, stated with the affine support
dimension in the preliminaries of
[Fradelizi--Guedon, The Extreme Points of Subsets of s-Concave Probabilities](https://perso.math.u-pem.fr/guedon.olivier/Articles/02/Fradelizi-Guedon.pdf).
The parameter conversion is the only classification input here.

For completeness, integrability makes the positive support bounded.
Choose an interior ball B(x0,rho) on which h is positive. If positive
support points x_j escaped to infinity, the balls
(x_j+B(x0,rho))/2 would contain a disjoint subsequence, and concavity
would give a fixed positive lower bound for h there. Their f-integrals
would have infinite sum. Similarly, if h(x_j) tended to infinity,
the SAME balls, now of fixed radius rho/2, would have h>=h(x_j)/2;
even a single such ball contradicts integral f=1 for large j.
Thus h and its support are bounded. The upper semicontinuous closure
of its hypograph provides the asserted concave boundary extension.
The boundary of the full q-dimensional support has H_q measure zero,
so this does not change mu. In the q=m case the constant density
also forces bounded support: an unbounded full-dimensional convex
set contains a disjoint sequence of equal-radius balls obtained in
the same way, and has infinite volume.

## 2. Exact ball representation, converse realization, and sharp exponent

Suppose 1<=q<m, identify E with R^q, and put r=m-q. Write kappa_r
for the volume of the unit Euclidean ball in R^r. Define

    L_f={(x,y): x in supp f,
                  |y| <= (f(x)/kappa_r)^(1/r)}.    (2)

Use the concave upper semicontinuous representative in (2). The
triangle inequality and concavity of the radius prove that L_f is
convex. Section 1 makes it compact; positivity of f in the support
interior makes it full m-dimensional. Fubini gives

    |L_f|=integral f=1,
    pi_#(1_(L_f) dx dy)=f(x)dx,                   (3)

where pi(x,y)=x. Thus projection of its uniform probability is
EXACTLY mu, not just an approximation.

Conversely, every such density is a normalized thin-body limit:
set L_epsilon={(x,epsilon y):(x,y) in L_f}. Then
|L_epsilon|=epsilon^r, its projected probability remains mu, and
its uniform probability converges weakly to mu on E. This follows
by bounded uniform continuity of test functions on the compact lift.
The construction embeds into R^D by choosing any r-dimensional
orthogonal complement to E. It realizes all the measures described
in Section 1.

If q=0, a shrinking m-ball realizes the Dirac limit and a fixed
m-ball projects to it. If q=m, the original limiting convex body K
with its NORMALIZED volume is already a realization. Its ordinary
volume need not be one: an m-dimensional volume-one body under the
identity projection cannot represent Uniform(K) unless |K|=1.
If a volume-one realization is wanted, one extra coordinate and
the prism K times [0,1/|K|] give it, in dimension m+1.

The exponent 1/r cannot be improved in general. On the standard
q-simplex take

    f(x)=c(1-x1-...-xq)^r,

with c chosen so integral f=1. Its r-th root is affine and nonnegative.
For every exponent beta>1/r, f^beta is a strictly convex nonconstant
power along an interior line, so it is not concave. Construction
(2) and its thin rescaling realize this example by m-dimensional
convex bodies.

More generally, (2) applies to a finite measure f dx of any positive
mass w: the lift then has volume w, and projection of its ordinary,
UNNORMALIZED volume is exactly that finite measure.

## 3. Exact failure of independent probability normalization

For epsilon>0, in continuous coordinates (x,y), use the actual three
fibers at integer bases -1,0,1

    K_-^epsilon=K_+^epsilon=[0,1] times [-epsilon/2,epsilon/2],
    K_0^epsilon=[0,2] times [-epsilon/2,epsilon/2].           (4)

Their lifted convex hull has EXACTLY these integer fibers. At the
middle base the forced endpoint midpoint is the smaller rectangle,
already contained in K_0^epsilon. The endpoint fibers are unchanged
because their base indices are exposed. Their areas are
(epsilon,2epsilon,epsilon), all tending to zero.

The separate normalized probability limits on the x-axis have densities

    f_-=f_+=1_[0,1],     f_0=(1/2)1_[0,2].        (5)

For m=2,q=1, the canonical unit-area lifts are

    L_-=L_+=[0,1] times [-1/2,1/2],
    L_0=[0,2] times [-1/4,1/4].                   (6)

They fail midpoint compatibility: (1/2,1/2) belongs to
(L_-+L_+)/2 but not to L_0.

In fact NO choice of full-dimensional equal-volume convex lifts
with the prescribed projection laws (5) can repair this. Suppose
|A_-|=|A_0|=|A_+|=1 and (A_-+A_+)/2 subset A_0. Brunn--Minkowski
forces equality of volumes and its equality case forces A_-,A_+
to be translates, with A_0 their midpoint body. Their projections
therefore all have the same interval length. The required endpoint
length one and middle length two contradict this. This argument
works in any common lift dimension, for a fixed projection to x.

This obstruction concerns independent PROBABILITY normalizations.
It does not obstruct preserving the relative masses. With the common
normalizer 4epsilon, the limiting densities are instead

    F_-=F_+=(1/4)1_[0,1],    F_0=(1/4)1_[0,2].   (7)

Their ball lifts are exactly compatible rectangles of common height
1/4 and lengths 1,2,1, with volumes 1/4,1/2,1/4. Equivalently,
the unnormalized weights (1,2,1) repair (5).

The body in (4) is an actual compatible thin family; it is not asserted
to have a full-dimensional Hausdorff hull limit. Its role is the exact
normalization obstruction, independent of that additional phenomenon.

## 4. A common-projection construction preserves compatibility exactly

Fix a single orthogonal decomposition R^m=R^q_x times R^r_y,
r=m-q>=1. Let a finite actual convex-compatible family K_z be given.
For every real x in pi(K_z), write

    a_z(x)=|K_z intersect ({x} times R^r)|_r.

For ONE common constant c>0 define

    K_z^#={(x,y): x in pi(K_z),
                       |y| <= (c a_z(x)/kappa_r)^(1/r)}.    (8)

Zero-volume nonempty sections give radius zero. Compactness of K_z
gives upper semicontinuity of the section volume; thus (8) is closed.
Each lift is convex by Brunn--Minkowski. More strongly, EVERY anchored
Minkowski inclusion is preserved:

    sum_i lambda_i K_(z_i) subset K_w,
    lambda_i>=0, sum_i lambda_i=1
          => sum_i lambda_i K_(z_i)^# subset K_w^#.        (9)

Indeed, at x=sum_i lambda_i x_i the original r-dimensional sections
have their Minkowski average inside the target section. Their volume
r-th roots obey Brunn--Minkowski, including nonempty zero-volume
sections. The target ball radius is therefore at least the weighted
sum of the source radii. The triangle inequality proves (9).
There is no choice of independent hidden directions in this argument:
the decomposition and the constant c are the SAME for all fibers.

Fubini also gives the exact identities

    |K_z^#|=c|K_z|,
    pi_#(1_(K_z^#) dx dy)=c pi_#(1_(K_z) dx dy).   (10)

Thus simultaneous ball replacement preserves every cap whose
continuous normal lies in R^q_x, including every tilt in the integer
base coordinates. It does not in general preserve caps with a
nonzero y-normal. Equations (9)--(10), rather than independent
probability lifts, are the valid finite-family compatibility identity.

## 5. Passing the common construction to a normalized thin limit

Here is a precise positive limit statement. Fix a finite base set P
and compatible families K_(z,l) contained in one bounded subset of
R^m. Put M_l=sum_(z in P)|K_(z,l)|. Suppose

    |K_(z,l)|/M_l -> w_z>0,
    pi_#(1_(K_(z,l)) dx)/M_l -> nu_z              (11)

weakly, for every z in P, and each nu_z has full q-dimensional
affine support in the COMMON projection R^q. No lower bound on M_l
is assumed. Apply (8) with c=1/M_l and denote the result by L_(z,l).
Then L_(z,l) converges in Hausdorff distance to a full m-dimensional
convex body L_z. Its ordinary volume is w_z, its projection volume
law is nu_z, and all the inclusions (9) pass to the L_z. Each L_z
is exactly the canonical ball lift of the density of nu_z.

Here are the necessary compactness details. Full-dimensional support
of nu_z supplies q+1 small neighborhoods of affinely independent
support points, each of positive measure. By the lower Portmanteau
bound, pi(K_(z,l)) meets all these neighborhoods for large l. Convexity
therefore puts a fixed q-ball of radius rho_z>0 into every such
projection. The outer projections are bounded by the given container.

Let H be the maximum section radius of L_(z,l). At a point attaining
H, average that point with the fixed projection ball. Concavity of
the radius gives radius at least H/2 on a q-ball of radius rho_z/2.
Since |L_(z,l)|=|K_(z,l)|/M_l<=1,

    1 >= kappa_r (H/2)^r kappa_q (rho_z/2)^q.      (12)

So all L_(z,l), over this finite set of z, lie in one compact set.
Blaschke selection gives simultaneous Hausdorff subsequential limits.
Volume continuity gives |L_z|=w_z>0, hence full dimension. Indicators
then converge almost everywhere away from the boundary of L_z, so
their volume measures and projected measures converge to those of
L_z. By (10)--(11), the latter are precisely nu_z.

Every L_(z,l) is invariant under all rotations of the hidden R^r
coordinate. Its limit is too, so each section is a centered ball.
The projected density specifies that ball radius almost everywhere;
concavity gives equality at every interior projection point, and
taking the closure of the body's interior fixes its boundary as well.
Thus the limiting body is unique. Every subsequence has this same
limit, proving convergence of the whole sequence. Minkowski sums are
continuous under Hausdorff convergence, so (9) survives exactly.

For q=0 the analogous assertion is simply the convergence of centered
m-balls with volumes w_z; the radius bound is immediate. Section 5
is stated for positive limiting w_z. It does not silently treat a
zero-weight fiber as a full-dimensional positive-mass limit.

If the original weak limiting laws all live in one q-dimensional
affine continuous subspace on which pi is an affine isometry, their
pi-images in (11) identify their FULL laws. In that case the L_z give
a simultaneous convex representation of the entire surviving law.
When their affine support directions differ, a common projection
usually retains only projected laws; it need not preserve the original
ambient cap events. Neither Section 5 nor Borell's single-measure
classification supplies the missing identification in that case.

## 6. Direct cross-measure characterization and a common-support lift

There is also a direct statement requiring no approximating bodies.
Let 1<=q<m, r=m-q, and let nu_z=f_z dx be positive finite
1/m-concave measures with full q-dimensional affine supports in ONE
common R^q. Assume the following cross-base Brunn--Minkowski
inequality for every anchored finite combination under consideration:

    j=sum_i lambda_i z_i,   lambda_i>0, sum_i lambda_i=1,
    nu_j(sum_i lambda_i E_i)^(1/m)
                 >=sum_i lambda_i nu_(z_i)(E_i)^(1/m),      (13)

for all compact E_i of positive source measure. Zero coefficients
are omitted. In an actual convex-compatible approximating family,
(13) holds for ALL finite anchored combinations, not just combinations
which can be decomposed using intermediate integer bases.

Then the concave density representatives satisfy the EXACT stronger
cross-base relation

    f_j(sum_i lambda_i x_i)^(1/r)
                  >=sum_i lambda_i f_(z_i)(x_i)^(1/r).      (14)

Initially (14) is asserted for x_i in the interiors of the positive
supports; taking closures gives the equivalent inclusion of the
canonical ball lifts in (2). Consequently all such lifts, whose
volumes are the original masses nu_z(R^q), are convex-compatible.

To prove this, the usual positive-neighborhood argument applied to
(13) first shows that the Minkowski average of the source supports
lies in the target support. For interior source points x_i their
average x is interior to the target support. Borell's representatives
are continuous and positive at all these points. Apply (13) to
q-balls of radii epsilon a_i around x_i, with arbitrary a_i>0. Their
Minkowski average is the ball around x of radius
epsilon sum_i lambda_i a_i. Divide by
kappa_q^(1/m) epsilon^(q/m), and let epsilon tend to zero. This yields

    f_j(x)^(1/m) (sum_i lambda_i a_i)^(q/m)
       >=sum_i lambda_i f_(z_i)(x_i)^(1/m) a_i^(q/m).       (15)

The radii must be optimized; setting all a_i equal would lose the
needed exponent. Normalize sum_i lambda_i a_i=1, put p=q/m in (0,1),
b_i=f_(z_i)(x_i)^(1/r), and S=sum_i lambda_i b_i. Jensen for t^p,
with probabilities omega_i=lambda_i b_i/S, gives

    sum_i lambda_i b_i^(1-p) a_i^p
      =S sum_i omega_i (a_i/b_i)^p
      <=S (sum_i omega_i a_i/b_i)^p=S^(1-p).      (16)

Equality is attained at a_i=b_i/S. Optimizing (15) therefore gives
f_j(x)^(1/m)>=S^(r/m), which is precisely (14).

There is no almost-everywhere boundary gap in the lift conclusion.
The canonical convex lifts are closures of their interiors. The
inequality proved at interior projection points implies inclusion
for the corresponding interior lift points; approximating arbitrary
lift points by such points and taking closure gives the whole set
inclusion. This also handles nonzero boundary density traces.

Conversely, if the canonical lifts obey these inclusions, apply
ordinary m-dimensional Brunn--Minkowski to their intersections with
the cylinders E_i times R^r. Fubini proves (13). Thus (13) and
compatibility of the canonical common-weight lifts are equivalent.

### How actual normalized limits provide (13)

For a finite family of actual convex fibers, the Minkowski average
of the portions whose q-projections lie in E_i is contained in the
target portion over sum_i lambda_i E_i. Brunn--Minkowski in dimension
m proves (13) for the projected volume measures after dividing ALL
of them by the same positive normalizer. If these finite measures
converge weakly, repeat the open-neighborhood/closed-neighborhood
argument of Section 1 to pass (13) to their limits. No interchange
of densities and limits is required.

Consequently, whenever the surviving weak fiber measures all have
full q-dimensional supports in the same affine continuous subspace
after one affine-in-base shear, and their common-normalized limits
are positive, this construction gives an EXACT compatible m-dimensional
lift of their full laws. The support need not be the same convex set
in each fiber. Different relative masses are retained, not discarded.

For a finite induced lattice-convex base family, take the convex hull
of the integer lifts. All anchored finite inclusions show that its
integer fibers are exactly the specified lifts. The original mixed
law is the projection of its uniform-fiber mixed volume law. In
particular any halfspace-depth bound at a lifted point transfers to
its projected point: the inverse image of every original halfspace
is a halfspace of the same mass containing that lifted point. If
the halfspace's restriction to the original affine support is
constant, a containing cap instead includes the whole represented
law and the bound is immediate.
This is an exact projection statement, not a weak-limit assertion
about depths. Without a common support subspace, only the common
projected laws have been represented.

### The endpoint q=m is different

When q=m, the measures are constant densities c_z on convex supports
Q_z. The same small-ball argument, now linear in the radii, gives

    Q_j contains sum_i lambda_i Q_(z_i),
    c_j>=max_(i:lambda_i>0) c_(z_i).               (17)

These two conditions are also sufficient for (13), by ordinary
m-dimensional Brunn--Minkowski. They do NOT in general force all
c_z to be equal, so an m-dimensional ordinary-volume representation
with one common normalization cannot be inferred merely from (13).
If all c_z equal c, the original supports with common normalization
c already are the desired representation. Otherwise an additional
height coordinate with constant fiber heights c_z gives a convex
representation in dimension m+1 by (17), but raises the dimension.
For example c_-=c_+=1,c_0=2 on the same interval obey (17) while
they are not one common multiple of ordinary interval volume.
This qualification is separate from the q=m single-probability
realization in Section 2.

In the bounded actual thin-body setting with M_l->0, a positive
surviving fiber cannot have a full m-dimensional limiting measure
support in the ORIGINAL continuous space. Otherwise take a Hausdorff
subsequence of its original fibers. The limiting convex set contains
the support of its weak probability limit, hence is full dimensional
and has positive m-volume. Volume continuity contradicts the fact
that the original fiber volumes are at most M_l->0. Thus q<m in
that particular vanishing-mass application; this observation does
not assert that different surviving fibers have the same q or the
same support directions.

The exact rectangle constants and volume-normalization identities are
checked in `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_normalized_thin_ball_lifts.py`. The general measure,
convexity, and compactness arguments above are mathematical proofs,
not conclusions from a numerical screen.
